sources.title: INEHRM, History of Women in Mexico

sources.note: IMSS founded in 1943 for worker/family health care and social protection under Article 123.

sources.note: 2000 presidential party alternation followed earlier electoral reforms.

sources.title: National Institute of Indigenous Peoples, Indigenous languages in Mexico
sources.note: 2020 census counted over seven million speakers of Indigenous languages; Náhuatl and Maya are among the largest groups.

sources.title: National Institute of Indigenous Peoples, language and schooling
sources.note: Indigenous languages remain in use; education policy increasingly recognizes multilingual teaching.

sources.title: Mexican Agriculture Secretariat, From maize to tortilla

sources.note: Maize remains major food, with varied native maize and nutrition from nixtamalization.

sources.note: Census tables distinguish piped water, drainage and toilet facilities across years and states.

sources.title: INEGI, 2020 census sanitation definition
sources.note: A sanitary facility may be a flush toilet, latrine or pit; not all connect to a sewer.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

Mexico’s imported 1878 polygon is a map snapshot, not 1821 independence. The 1824 federal constitution, 1867 restoration and 1917 constitution are separately dated. No geometry or Indigenous-territory accuracy is certified.

Rural schooling, cuisine, toilet facilities and social insurance varied among places and families. Neither Spanish nor Náhuatl excerpt represents every Mexican language. Narrative awaits independent review.

proposedOverrides.summary: Mexico won independence in 1821 and established a federal republic in 1824, well before the imported 1878 map snapshot. Railways and the long Díaz presidency preceded the 1910 revolution and 1917 constitution; education, land and labor rights changed amid conflict. Indigenous communities and languages, everyday maize traditions, worker health insurance and electoral change are part of its continuing history. Mexico remains a republic.

identityEvidence.assessment: Imported label/interval confirmed; border and Indigenous-territory accuracy unverified.
